title: Why Good Working Relationships Sour and End When They Didn't Need To
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece maps out a recurring blueprint by which good working relationships deteriorate: an initial grievance goes unaddressed, a second incident compounds it, and both parties retreat into cold, indirect communication rather than naming what's actually bothering them. The author argues neither side reads the other's nonverbal cues as intended, which lets misunderstanding and resentment spiral for weeks or months until the relationship collapses through resignation or termination. The prescribed fix is early, direct conversation about what's bothering you before the pattern takes hold.
points: Relationships sour through a predictable pattern: an unaddressed grievance, a second incident, then a retreat into cold, indirect communication instead of direct conversation.
Both parties typically misread each other's nonverbal signals during the cold-war phase, each assuming the other is oblivious rather than upset.
The negative spiral is self-reinforcing — each new slight adds to unspoken resentment that neither side will name out loud.
The prescribed fix is to address what's bothering you early, before avoidance and silence let the pattern take root.
quotes: We have all experienced or seen a solid working relationship sour and end without understanding exactly how it happened.
Instead of discussing their displeasure with the team member, the leader keeps their disappointment bottled up.
Of course, the team member is not a mind reader and remains mostly oblivious to what is going on.
What was once a productive working relationship now looks like the Cold War.
Confronting bad behavior or poor choices before they infect the relationship and create a downward spiral is crucially important in all relationships.
